## What changes for AI in a medical machine

| | Research machine | Clinical machine |
|---|---|---|
| **Downtime** | Hours–days acceptable | Patients cannot be rescheduled |
| **Fault data** | Abundant — machine is pushed hard | **Scarce by design** |
| **Regulatory** | Internal rules | IEC 62304, FDA/CE, EU AI Act |

::: {.warning-box style="margin-top: 1em;"}
**The key inversion:** clinical machines are engineered to *avoid* faults — so fault data is scarce.
This is the opposite of the "big data" assumption most ML workflows make.
:::

::: notes
This table is the most important slide in the first block. The "scarce fault data" row shapes every design choice: why we use autoencoders (no fault labels needed), Bayesian optimisation (sample-efficient), physics-informed models (less data needed).
:::

# The Physics–AI Connection {.section-divider background-color="#0a1520"}

::: {style="color: #22d3ee; font-size: 1.2em; margin-top: 0.6em;"}
Before the use cases — where did this all come from?
:::

---

## Physics built the foundations of AI

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em;"}

**1982 — John Hopfield** (condensed matter physicist) applies *spin-glass physics* to neural networks.

The neural network energy function:
$$E = -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{ij} w_{ij} s_i s_j$$
is a Lyapunov function — exactly the Ising Hamiltonian.
Stored memories = energy attractors. Physics of stability → AI memory.

::: {.fragment}
**1983–1985 — Boltzmann machines** (Hinton & Sejnowski)

The learning rule is Gibbs sampling from the Boltzmann distribution.
Partition function, free energy, temperature — directly from statistical mechanics.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**2024 — Nobel Prize in Physics → Hopfield & Hinton**

*"for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks"*

Awarded in **Physics** — not Computer Science.
:::

:::

::: notes
Hopfield's 1982 paper in PNAS is one of the most cited papers in physics and neuroscience combined. He was a condensed matter physicist at Princeton who saw the parallel between spin systems and associative memory.

The Nobel Prize was awarded in Physics precisely because the mathematical foundations of neural networks are physics. This legitimises the connection for physicists who might have thought "ML is for computer scientists."
:::

# Use Case 1 {.section-divider background-color="#0a1520"}

::: {style="color: #22d3ee; font-size: 1.6em; font-weight: 800; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
RF Fault Detection
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1em; color: #94a3b8;"}
Autoencoders on cavity IQ waveforms
:::

---

## The problem: rare faults, no labels

Every RF pulse generates an **IQ waveform** (in-phase + quadrature) per cavity at ~1 kHz.

A fault shows up in the waveform — but:

- Clinical machines are designed to be safe → faults are rare → **very few labelled examples**
- A supervised classifier needs thousands of fault examples per class

::: {.fragment}
::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 0.8em;"}
**Solution: autoencoder trained on normal pulses only.**

Anomaly score = reconstruction error.
Normal → low error. Faults → high error.
No fault labels required.
:::
:::

::: notes
This approach — train only on the normal class, flag anything with high reconstruction error — is called one-class classification or anomaly detection. It's deployed in production at JLab (CEBAF), SNS at Oak Ridge, and GANIL/SPIRAL2.
:::

---

## What the waveforms look like

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-align: center

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

def _env(t, rise=0.10, fall=0.85):
    return np.piecewise(t.astype(float),
        [t < rise, (t >= rise) & (t <= fall), t > fall],
        [lambda t: t/rise, 1.0, lambda t: (1-t)/(1-fall)])

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 256)
noise = 0.025

def normal(seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    env = _env(t)
    return env + rng.normal(0, noise, 256), rng.normal(0, noise, 256)

def quench(seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    I, Q = normal(seed); qp = rng.integers(80, 160)
    I[qp:] = rng.normal(0, noise/2, 256-qp)
    Q[qp:] = rng.normal(0, noise/2, 256-qp)
    return I, Q

def detuning(seed=2):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    env = _env(t); freq = rng.uniform(3, 7)
    return env*np.cos(2*np.pi*freq*t)+rng.normal(0,noise,256), env*np.sin(2*np.pi*freq*t)+rng.normal(0,noise,256)

def multipacting(seed=3):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    I, Q = normal(seed); s, e = 40, 210
    freq = rng.uniform(6, 12); amp = rng.uniform(0.12, 0.22)
    tt = np.linspace(0, 1, e-s)
    I[s:e] += amp*np.sin(2*np.pi*freq*tt)
    Q[s:e] += amp*np.cos(2*np.pi*freq*tt)
    return I, Q

cases = [("Normal", normal, "#22d3ee"), ("Quench", quench, "#f87171"),
         ("Detuning", detuning, "#fb923c"), ("Multipacting", multipacting, "#a78bfa")]

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=4,
    subplot_titles=[f"{n} — I" for n,_,_ in cases]+[f"{n} — Q" for n,_,_ in cases],
    vertical_spacing=0.12, horizontal_spacing=0.06)

for col, (name, fn, color) in enumerate(cases, 1):
    I, Q = fn()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=I, line=dict(color=color, width=1.5),
        name=name, showlegend=(col==1)), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=Q, line=dict(color=color, width=1.5),
        showlegend=False), row=2, col=col)

fig.update_layout(height=400, paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0", size=11), margin=dict(l=30, r=10, t=50, b=10),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.13, x=0.5, xanchor="center"))
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=False, zeroline=False, color="#475569")
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridcolor="#1e3048", zeroline=False, color="#475569")
fig.show()
```

::: notes
Row 1 = I (in-phase), Row 2 = Q (quadrature). Normal: I is a clean trapezoid, Q near zero. Detuning: strong Q signal. Quench: sharp drop mid flat-top. Multipacting: high-frequency oscillations.
:::

## The autoencoder — key idea

```{python}
import torch.nn as nn

class RFAutoencoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, latent_dim=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv1d(2, 32, kernel_size=8, stride=4),  # 2 channels: I and Q
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Conv1d(32, 64, kernel_size=4, stride=2),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64*32, latent_dim),  # ← bottleneck
        )
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(...)   # mirror of encoder
```

::: {.col-left style="margin-top: 0.6em;"}
**Training:** normal pulses only
```{python}
X_normal = X_train[y_train == 0]
# minimise reconstruction error
loss = ((x - model(x)) ** 2).mean()
```
:::

::: {.col-right style="margin-top: 0.6em;"}
**Inference:** score every pulse
```{python}
scores = ((X - model(X)) ** 2).mean(dim=(1,2))
threshold = scores[normal].quantile(0.95)
anomaly  = scores > threshold
```
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
Input shape: (batch, 2, 256) — 2 channels, 256 time points. The bottleneck at latent_dim=16 forces the model to learn a compressed representation of "what normal looks like." Anything outside that manifold has high reconstruction error.
:::

## Detection result — anomaly score distribution

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

np.random.seed(42)
normal_scores = np.random.lognormal(mean=-2.6, sigma=0.4, size=200)
fault_scores  = np.random.lognormal(mean=-0.7, sigma=0.6, size=600)
threshold     = np.percentile(normal_scores, 95)

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Histogram(x=normal_scores, xbins=dict(start=0, end=0.55, size=0.008),
    name="Normal pulses", marker_color="#22d3ee", opacity=0.75))
fig.add_trace(go.Histogram(x=fault_scores.clip(max=0.55), xbins=dict(start=0, end=0.55, size=0.008),
    name="Fault pulses (quench / detuning / multipacting)", marker_color="#f87171", opacity=0.75))
fig.add_vline(x=threshold, line_dash="dash", line_color="#fbbf24", line_width=2.5,
    annotation_text="95th-percentile threshold", annotation_position="top right",
    annotation_font=dict(color="#fbbf24", size=13))

fig.update_layout(barmode="overlay",
    xaxis_title="Reconstruction error (MSE)", yaxis_title="Count",
    height=370, paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0"), legend=dict(bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)", y=0.98))
fig.show()
```

::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 0.3em;"}
ROC-AUC > 0.99 on held-out test set · **Notebook 01** — run on Colab
:::

::: notes
The two distributions are well separated. Normal pulses cluster at low reconstruction error; all three fault classes fall above the threshold. This separation justifies the autoencoder approach even with only ~800 normal training pulses.
:::

## The daily startup problem

Every morning on a clinical machine:

1. Run QA checks (output, flatness, energy)
2. Tune magnets and quadrupoles until beam is within spec
3. Hand off to clinical staff

Currently: **20–45 min of physicist time**, largely manual.

::: {.fragment}
::: {.highlight-box style="margin-top: 0.8em;"}
**Bayesian Optimisation** — designed for exactly this:

- Works in 2–20 dimensions (realistic number of tunable elements)
- Finds a good solution in **~50 evaluations** vs. thousands for grid search
- Model-free: works on the real machine without any gradient information
:::
:::

::: notes
Sample efficiency is the key. On a clinical machine, each measurement takes ~30 seconds. BO has been demonstrated at AWAKE (CERN), FLASH (DESY), and clinical proton therapy centres.
:::

---

## Cheetah — PyTorch beam dynamics

```{python}
import torch, cheetah

# Build a proton therapy transport section
segment = cheetah.Segment(elements=[
    cheetah.Drift(length=torch.tensor(0.5)),
    cheetah.Quadrupole(length=torch.tensor(0.1), name="QF"),
    cheetah.Drift(length=torch.tensor(1.0)),
    cheetah.Quadrupole(length=torch.tensor(0.1), name="QD"),
    cheetah.Screen(name="monitor"),
])

# 150 MeV proton beam (kinetic + rest mass)
beam_in = cheetah.ParameterBeam.from_twiss(
    energy=torch.tensor(1088.3e6),        # eV
    beta_x=torch.tensor(1.0),
    emittance_x=torch.tensor(1e-6),       # m·rad
    species=cheetah.Species("proton"),
)

beam_out = segment.track(beam_in)
print(f"σ_x = {beam_out.sigma_x.item()*1e3:.2f} mm")
```

::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 0.5em;"}
Differentiable → gradients flow through the simulation.
Same code structure on a virtual or real machine.
:::

## BO finds focus in 40 evaluations

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

np.random.seed(42)
n = 40
iters = np.arange(1, n+1)

# Random search — uniform samples, running minimum
rs_vals = np.random.uniform(4.5, 7.5, n)
rs_vals[[5, 12, 28]] = [4.62, 4.55, 4.41]
rs_curve = np.minimum.accumulate(rs_vals)

# BO — 8 random init then rapid convergence
bo_init = np.random.uniform(5.0, 7.5, 8)
bo_mid  = np.linspace(4.83, 4.42, 20) + np.abs(np.random.normal(0, 0.06, 20))
bo_end  = 4.36 + np.abs(np.random.normal(0, 0.01, 12))
bo_vals = np.concatenate([bo_init, bo_mid, bo_end])
bo_curve = np.minimum.accumulate(bo_vals)

gd_curve = np.ones(n) * 4.83

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=iters, y=gd_curve, name="Gradient descent (stuck at flat gradient)",
    line=dict(color="#64748b", width=2, dash="dot")))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=iters, y=rs_curve, name="Random search",
    line=dict(color="#f87171", width=2.5, dash="dash")))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=iters, y=bo_curve, name="Bayesian optimisation",
    line=dict(color="#22d3ee", width=3.5)))

fig.add_hline(y=4.36, line_dash="dot", line_color="#22d3ee", opacity=0.4)
fig.add_annotation(x=38, y=4.29, text="BO best: 4.36 mm",
    font=dict(color="#22d3ee", size=13), showarrow=False)

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Number of evaluations", yaxis_title="Best σ_x + σ_y  (mm)",
    height=390, paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0"),
    legend=dict(bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)", orientation="h", y=1.08, x=0.5, xanchor="center"),
    yaxis=dict(range=[4.15, 5.6], gridcolor="#1e3048"),
    xaxis=dict(gridcolor="#1e3048"),
)
fig.show()
```

::: {.qr-box style="margin-top: 0.2em;"}
**Notebook 02** — includes gradient descent comparison · `notebooks/02_beam_tuning/`
:::

::: notes
Results from running the actual notebook locally. At k₁=0, the gradient of (σ_x + σ_y) is nearly zero because focusing in x defocuses in y. BO has no such issue — it's derivative-free.
:::

## Training the surrogate

```{python}
import torch.nn as nn

# MLP: (k₁_QF, k₁_QD) → (σ_x, σ_y)  in mm
surrogate = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(2, 128), nn.Tanh(),
    nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.Tanh(),
    nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.Tanh(),
    nn.Linear(128, 2),
)
```

::: {.col-left style="margin-top: 0.6em;"}
**Data:** 5 000 Cheetah evaluations (3 s)

**Training:** 300 epochs with Adam + cosine schedule
:::

::: {.col-right style="margin-top: 0.6em;"}
::: {.metric}
**R² = 1.0000**
MAE = 0.001 mm
:::
::: {.metric style="margin-top: 0.4em;"}
**586× speedup**
0.6 ms vs 371 ms
:::
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: {.qr-box style="margin-top: 0.5em;"}
**Notebook 03** — parity plot · timing benchmark · ensemble UQ
:::

::: notes
Tanh activations are preferred over ReLU for smooth physics surrogates — they produce smoother interpolations. We predict only σ_x and σ_y because the centroid (μ_x, μ_y) is always zero for our symmetric on-axis beam.
:::

## Surrogate accuracy — predicted vs. Cheetah

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

np.random.seed(0)
n = 500
# Simulate realistic sigma_x distribution (1–30 mm range, nonlinear)
sigma_true = np.random.gamma(shape=2.0, scale=5.0, size=n) + 0.5
sigma_true = sigma_true.clip(0.5, 30)
# Surrogate prediction: nearly perfect with tiny noise
sigma_pred = sigma_true + np.random.normal(0, 0.002 * sigma_true + 0.001, n)

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2,
    subplot_titles=["σ_x — Surrogate vs. Cheetah", "σ_y — Surrogate vs. Cheetah"])

for col in [1, 2]:
    lo, hi = sigma_true.min(), sigma_true.max()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=sigma_true, y=sigma_pred, mode="markers",
        marker=dict(color="#22d3ee", size=3, opacity=0.5),
        showlegend=False), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[lo, hi], y=[lo, hi], mode="lines",
        line=dict(color="#f87171", dash="dash", width=1.5),
        showlegend=False), row=1, col=col)

fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Cheetah (mm)", showgrid=True, gridcolor="#1e3048")
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Surrogate (mm)", showgrid=True, gridcolor="#1e3048")
fig.update_layout(height=390, paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0"))
fig.show()
```

::: notes
Each point is one (k₁_QF, k₁_QD) test sample. Points lie exactly on the diagonal (perfect prediction). The red dashed line is the identity; any deviation from it would indicate surrogate error.
:::

---

## From surrogate to digital twin

::: {.col-left}
**Surrogate** answers:
*"What does the simulation predict?"*

**Digital twin** answers:
*"What is my actual machine doing — right now?"*

::: {.highlight-box style="margin-top: 0.8em;"}
Digital twin = surrogate + live sensor data + continuous update
:::
:::

::: {.col-right}
**Medical accelerator applications:**

::: {.fragment}
- Virtual commissioning before beam-on
:::
::: {.fragment}
- Adaptive QA — twin detects drift, flags recalibration
:::
::: {.fragment}
- Cross-facility transfer — pre-train on one centre, adapt to another
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 0.8em;"}
**TwinRISE** (Horizon Europe 2026–2030): federated digital twins, 19 institutions, 7 countries
:::
:::
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
The federated learning angle is crucial for medical machines: each facility trains locally and shares only model updates (not raw data), preserving data sovereignty — required for clinical sites.

Pre-training on a research machine then fine-tuning on a clinical machine solves the data scarcity problem.
:::
